summary: "De Saint-Louis à Tripoli par le Lac Tchad" by P.-L. Monteil is a travel and exploration narrative written in the late 19th century. It recounts a French officer’s trans-African journey from Senegal to Tripoli via Lake Chad, blending route-finding, diplomacy, and on-the-ground reporting across the Soudan and the Sahara. The focus is the reconnaissance of the Say–Barroua boundary and negotiations with West African polities such as Sokoto and Bornu while proving that a small, disciplined escort can traverse the interior. Expect first-hand logistics, political context, and pointed reflections on contemporary imperial expeditions. The opening of the book frames the expedition’s stakes: an author’s foreword acknowledges a hurried composition and limited scientific detail, followed by Melchior de Vogüé’s preface situating the mission in the context of the Franco-British convention, earlier explorers, and France’s excitement over Monteil’s reappearance. Monteil then states his method—ten armed men, speed, and persuasion—contrasts it with a critical review of Stanley’s Emin Pasha expedition, and outlines his modest funding and lean armament. He recruits the loyal Badaire, departs France for Dakar and Saint-Louis, ascends the Senegal to Khayes, and marches across the Soudan through Bafoulabé, Kita, Koundou, Bamako, and Koulikoro, splitting his convoy before reaching Ségou to finalize preparations. After describing camp routine and local allies at Ségou, the narrative turns east: a tense New Year’s Eve at Fatené is defused by fortification and vigilance, a swift push secures the Bani crossing ahead of rumored attackers, and at San he negotiates and signs a treaty with the Almamy Alassana, closing with a concise sketch of San’s trade role and the surrounding political landscape.
